<!-- theorem-1: body_md -->
\label{thm:main-existence}
For every $n\ge5$, $\mathcal A_n$ is finite free of rank $4(n+3)$ over $R$, its special fibre is $A_n$, and
$\mathcal A_n\otimes_RK\cong
 K^{7}\times \operatorname{M}_2(K)^{n-1}\times\operatorname{M}_3(K)$.
For $n=4$, $\mathcal A_4$ is finite free of rank $27$ and
$\mathcal A_4\otimes_RK\cong
 K^{6}\times\operatorname{M}_2(K)^3\times\operatorname{M}_3(K)$.
Consequently, $A_n\rightsquigarrow K^{7}\times\operatorname{M}_2(K)^{n-1}\times\operatorname{M}_3(K)
 \quad(n\ge5)$
in the equivalent deformation senses of \cite[Theorem~2.20]{JS2026}, with the displayed $n=4$ modification.
<!-- end theorem-1 -->
<!-- theorem-2: body_md -->
\label{thm:main-unique}
Let $S$ be a finite-dimensional semisimple $\Bbbk$-algebra to which $A_n$ flatly deforms.
Then
\[
 S\cong
 \begin{cases}
 \Bbbk^6\times\operatorname{M}_2(\Bbbk)^3\times\operatorname{M}_3(\Bbbk),&n=4,\\[1mm]
 \Bbbk^7\times\operatorname{M}_2(\Bbbk)^{n-1}\times\operatorname{M}_3(\Bbbk),&n\ge5.
 \end{cases}
\]
In particular the semisimple deformation is unique up to isomorphism.
<!-- end theorem-2 -->
<!-- lemma-1: body_md -->
\label{lem:topNak}
Let $R=\Bbbk[[t]]$, let
$\widehat F=R\langle\!\langle x_1,\ldots,x_r\rangle\!\rangle$,
and let $\mathcal B=\widehat F/J$ for a closed two-sided ideal $J$.
Put $\mathfrak n=(x_1,\ldots,x_r)\mathcal B$ and suppose
$B_0:=\mathcal B/t\mathcal B$
is finite dimensional over $\Bbbk$ and $B_0/\overline{\mathfrak n}\cong\Bbbk$.
Let $d=\dim_\Bbbk B_0$ and $K_0=\Bbbk((t))$.
Then:
\begin{enumerate}[label=\rm(\roman*)]
\item $\mathcal B$ is a finite $R$-module and is $t$-adically complete and separated;
\item $\dim_{K_0}(\mathcal B\otimes_RK_0)\le d$;
\item if $\mathcal B\otimes_RK_0$ has a quotient of $K_0$-dimension $d$, then $\mathcal B$ is free of rank $d$ over $R$ and that quotient map is an isomorphism.
\end{enumerate}
The same conclusions hold after any algebraic extension of $K_0$, in particular over $K=\Bbbk\{\!\{t\}\!\}$.
<!-- end lemma-1 -->
<!-- proof-1: body_md -->
Let $I=(t)+\mathfrak n$.  Since $B_0$ is a finite-dimensional local algebra, its radical $\overline{\mathfrak n}$ is nilpotent.  Hence there exists $N$ such that
$\mathfrak n^N\subseteq t\mathcal B$.
Every product of $N$ elements of $I$ either contains a factor $t$ or lies in $\mathfrak n^N$, so
$I^N\subseteq t\mathcal B$.
Iterating gives
$I^{Nq}\subseteq t^q\mathcal B\subseteq I^q$ for $q\ge1$.
Thus the $I$-adic and $t$-adic topologies on $\mathcal B$ are equivalent.  Since $J$ is closed and $\widehat F$ is $I$-adically complete and separated, so is $\mathcal B$, and therefore $\mathcal B$ is $t$-adically complete and separated.

Choose $e_1,\ldots,e_d\in\mathcal B$ lifting a $\Bbbk$-basis of $B_0$.
Modulo $t$ they span, hence
\[
 \mathcal B=Re_1+\cdots+Re_d+t\mathcal B.
\]
Starting with any $b\in\mathcal B$, choose coefficients modulo $t$, then correct the error modulo $t^2$, and continue inductively.  Completeness of $R$ and $\mathcal B$ makes the coefficient sequences converge, giving $b=\sum_{i=1}^d a_i(t)e_i, a_i(t)\in R$.
Therefore $R^d\twoheadrightarrow\mathcal B$, proving (i), and tensoring with $K_0$ proves (ii).

Since $R$ is a DVR, the structure theorem for finite $R$-modules gives
\[
 \mathcal B\cong R^s\oplus\bigoplus_{j=1}^{q}R/(t^{a_j}),
 \qquad a_j\ge1.
\]
Consequently, $\dim_\Bbbk B_0=s+q,
 \dim_{K_0}(\mathcal B\otimes_RK_0)=s$.
If the generic fibre has a quotient of dimension $d=s+q$, then (ii) forces $s=d$ and hence $q=0$.  Thus $\mathcal B\cong R^d$, and a surjection between two $d$-dimensional generic fibres is an isomorphism.  Scalar extension does not change the argument.
<!-- end proof-1 -->
<!-- remark-1: body_md -->
\Cref{lem:topNak} shows that flatness need not be checked before constructing the generic fibre.  It is enough to produce a semisimple quotient whose dimension already equals that of the special fibre.
<!-- end remark-1 -->
<!-- proposition-1: body_md -->
\label{prop:scalar}
For every $n\ge5$, \eqref{eq:H} has exactly seven roots of positive $t$-valuation, counted without multiplicity, and all have valuation $4/7$.  They give seven pairwise nonisomorphic one-dimensional representations of $B_n$.
For $n=4$ there are exactly six positive-valuation roots.
<!-- end proposition-1 -->
<!-- proof-2: body_md -->
For $n\ge5$ expand $H_n(z)=n^2z^{2n-2}+2ntz^{n+1}-2nt^2z^{n-1}
 +t^2z^4-2t^3z^2+t^4+3z^7$.
The first lower Newton edge joins $(0,4)$ to $(7,0)$; every other displayed point lies strictly above that edge or on the horizontal continuation.  The edge polynomial is $1+3u^7$,
which is separable in characteristic zero.  Newton--Puiseux therefore gives exactly seven distinct roots with $v_t(z)=4/7$.  The remaining roots have valuation zero and do not belong to the completed local branch.  From $Q_n(z)^2=-3z^7$ one obtains $v_t(a)=6/7>0$.

For $n=4$, put $t=s^3$ and $z=s^2u$.  Dividing \eqref{eq:H} by $s^{12}$ gives
\[
 (4u^3-1+su^2)^2+3s^2u^7=0.
\]
At $s=0$ the three roots $u_0^3=1/4$ are double.  Write $u=u_0+sv+O(s^2)$.  The first nonzero coefficient is
\[
 u_0^4\bigl((12v+1)^2+3u_0^3\bigr)
 =u_0^4\bigl((12v+1)^2+3/4\bigr),
\]
which has two distinct roots in $v$.  Thus each $u_0$ splits into two Puiseux branches, giving six distinct positive-valuation roots.
<!-- end proof-2 -->
<!-- proposition-2: body_md -->
\label{prop:two}
For $n\ge5$, \eqref{eq:P} has exactly $n-1$ distinct positive-valuation Puiseux roots.  Each root yields an irreducible representation
\[
 B_n\twoheadrightarrow\operatorname{M}_2(K),
\]
and the resulting $n-1$ simple modules are pairwise nonisomorphic.
For $n=4$ the same construction gives three such branches.
<!-- end proposition-2 -->
<!-- proof-3: body_md -->
For $n=5$ the Newton points $(0,2),(2,1),(4,0)$ are collinear, giving four roots of valuation $1/2$.
For $n\ge6$ the lower polygon has two edges
\[
 (0,2)\longrightarrow(2,1),
 \qquad
 (2,1)\longrightarrow(n-1,0).
\]
Thus two roots have valuation $1/2$ and $n-3$ roots have valuation $1/(n-3)$.  The edge polynomials
\[
 2u^2-(1+\omega),
 \qquad
 n(1+\omega^{n-3})u^{n-3}+2
\]
are separable.  For $n=4$ the single lower edge joins $(0,2)$ to $(3,0)$ and gives three roots of valuation $2/3$.

For any such root define
$\Delta_\lambda=-\frac{\lambda^3}{3}-a_\lambda^2,
b_\lambda^2=\Delta_\lambda$,
and
\begin{equation*}
 X_\lambda=
 \begin{pmatrix}a_\lambda&b_\lambda\\ b_\lambda&-a_\lambda\end{pmatrix}.
\end{equation*}
Then $X_\lambda^2=-\lambda^3I_2/3$, so \eqref{eq:r1} holds.  In \eqref{eq:r2} the off-diagonal coefficient of $X_{ij}$ is
\[
 \lambda_i^2+\lambda_i\lambda_j+\lambda_j^2,
\]
which vanishes for $(\lambda_i,\lambda_j)=(\lambda,\omega\lambda)$; the diagonal equations are exactly \eqref{eq:P}.

It remains to see $b_\lambda\ne0$.  For $n=5$, the edge polynomial in $u^2$ has discriminant $24$,
so all four roots are simple. In every branch with $n\ge5$,
$v_t(a_\lambda)\ge1$ and $v_t(\lambda^3)\le3/2<2$.
Thus $v_t(a_\lambda^2)>v_t(\lambda^3)$.  The $n=4$ valuation check is identical to the one-edge calculation and gives $\Delta_\lambda\ne0$.  Thus $Y_\lambda$ has two distinct eigenspaces and $X_\lambda$ connects them, so the representation is irreducible.  Burnside's theorem gives the full image $\operatorname{M}_2(K)$.
Distinct $\lambda$ give distinct spectra of $Y_\lambda$, hence pairwise nonisomorphic modules.
<!-- end proof-3 -->
<!-- proposition-3: body_md -->
\label{prop:three}
For every $n\ge4$, $B_n$ has an irreducible three-dimensional representation and hence a quotient $\operatorname{M}_3(K)$.
<!-- end proposition-3 -->
<!-- proof-4: body_md -->
Put $v_i=a_i+r$ and write $\mathbf1=(1,1,1)^T$.  Since $\sum a_i=-r$, we have $\sum v_i=2r$.  Define
$X=\mathbf1(v_0,v_1,v_2)-rI_3$.
If $U=\mathbf1(v_0,v_1,v_2)$, then $U^2=2rU$, so
$X^2=U^2-2rU+r^2I_3=r^2I_3=-\frac c3I_3$.
Since $Y^3=cI_3$, relation \eqref{eq:r1} holds.  The diagonal entry $X_{ii}$ is $a_i$, so the diagonal part of \eqref{eq:r2} vanishes by definition.  If $i\ne j$, then
$\lambda_i^2+\lambda_i\lambda_j+\lambda_j^2=0$,
so the off-diagonal part vanishes as well.

Finally $v_t(\lambda_i)=2/3$, hence the $t^2/\lambda_i^2$ term shows $v_t(a_i)=2/3$, while $v_t(r)=1$.  Thus $v_i=a_i+r\ne0$ for all $i$.  Since $Y$ has three distinct eigenvalues, any common invariant subspace is the span of a subset of the three eigenspaces; the nonzero off-diagonal entries of $X$ rule out every proper nonempty subset.  The representation is irreducible, and Burnside's theorem gives image $\operatorname{M}_3(K)$.
<!-- end proof-4 -->
<!-- proposition-4: body_md -->
\label{prop:center-count}
For the completed local Jacobi algebras $A_n$,
\[
 \dim_\Bbbk Z(A_n)=
 \begin{cases}
 10,&n=4,\\
 n+7,&n\ge5.
 \end{cases}
\]
<!-- end proposition-4 -->
<!-- proof-5: body_md -->
The uniform proof is \cref{thm:cyc-rank}.  It begins with the two relations
\[
 r_x=3x^2+y^3,
 \qquad
 r_y=y^2x+yxy+xy^2+n y^{n-1}.
\]
The six-letter overlap in \cref{app:center} yields the two terminal
cyclic relations \eqref{eq:cyc-terminal} for all congruence classes
of $n-1$ modulo three.  Together with the $12$-word spanning
reduction, these show $\dim\operatorname{HH}_0(A_n)\le n+7$ for $n\ge5$
and $\dim\operatorname{HH}_0(A_4)\le10$; the $n=5$ endpoint is handled
by its distinct relations involving $[y^9],[y^{10}],[y^{11}]$.
The finite free deformation of Theorem~\ref{thm:main-existence} has
exactly $n+7$ simple blocks for $n\ge5$ and ten for $n=4$,
so specialization gives the reverse inequality.
Since $A_n$ is symmetric, $Z(A_n)\cong\operatorname{HH}_0(A_n)^*$.
The resulting bases and the rank increment are stated in
Theorem~\ref{thm:cyc-rank}.
<!-- end proof-5 -->
<!-- remark-2: body_md -->
\label{rem:center-audit}
The rank formula is proved by uniform terminal cyclic identities
and saturation by a separately constructed flat family; it does
not rely on extrapolating row-echelon pivots from finitely many $n$.
The $n=4$ length follows from terminal relations and dimension
saturation in \cref{app:four}.
<!-- end remark-2 -->
<!-- lemma-2: body_md -->
\label{lem:h1h2}
Let $A$ be a finite-dimensional symmetric $\Bbbk$-algebra satisfying
\[
 \Omega^4_{A^e}(A)\cong A
\]
in the stable bimodule category.  Then
$\dim_\Bbbk\operatorname{HH}^1(A,A)=\dim_\Bbbk\operatorname{HH}^2(A,A)$.
In particular this holds for every contraction algebra $A_n$.
<!-- end lemma-2 -->
<!-- proof-6: body_md -->
For a symmetric algebra, Tate duality gives a perfect pairing
\cite[\S2]{Linckelmann2013}
\[
 \widehat{\operatorname{HH}}^{q}(A,A)\times
 \widehat{\operatorname{HH}}^{-q-1}(A,A)\longrightarrow\Bbbk.
\]
Taking $q=1$ yields
\[
 \dim\operatorname{HH}^1(A,A)=\dim\widehat{\operatorname{HH}}^{-2}(A,A).
\]
Four-periodicity gives
\[
 \widehat{\operatorname{HH}}^{-2}(A,A)\cong\widehat{\operatorname{HH}}^{2}(A,A)=\operatorname{HH}^2(A,A),
\]
where the last equality uses positive degree.
<!-- end proof-6 -->
<!-- lemma-3: body_md -->
\label{lem:smooth-criterion}
Let $A$ be a $d$-dimensional algebra and suppose that $A$ deforms to a semisimple algebra $S$ of dimension $d$.  If
\[
 \dim Z(A)=\dim Z(S)
 \quad\text{and}\quad
 \dim\operatorname{HH}^1(A,A)=\dim\operatorname{HH}^2(A,A),
\]
then $[A]\in\mathcal M_d$ is a smooth point.
<!-- end lemma-3 -->
<!-- proof-7: body_md -->
The tangent space to $\mathcal M_d$ at $A$ is the space of normalized Hochschild $2$-cocycles, while the tangent space to the $G$-orbit is the space of normalized $2$-coboundaries.  Hence
\begin{equation}\label{eq:tangentdim}
 \dim T_{[A]}\mathcal M_d=\dim O_A+h^2(A).
\end{equation}
Moreover
\[
 \operatorname{Der}(A)/\operatorname{Inn}(A)=\operatorname{HH}^1(A,A),
 \qquad
 \dim\operatorname{Inn}(A)=d-\dim Z(A),
\]
so
\begin{equation}\label{eq:orbitdim}
 \dim O_A=\dim G-d+\dim Z(A)-h^1(A).
\end{equation}
Since $S$ is semisimple, $h^1(S)=0$, and therefore
\[
 \dim O_S=\dim G-d+\dim Z(S).
\]
Combining the hypotheses with \eqref{eq:tangentdim}--\eqref{eq:orbitdim} gives
\[
 \dim T_{[A]}\mathcal M_d=\dim O_S.
\]
The deformation implies $[A]\in\overline{O_S}$ (equivalently by \cite[Theorem~2.20]{JS2026}), so the local dimension of $\mathcal M_d$ at $[A]$ is at least $\dim O_S$.  Local dimension is always bounded above by tangent dimension.  Hence equality holds, the local ring is regular, and $[A]$ is smooth.
<!-- end proof-7 -->
<!-- corollary-1: body_md -->
\label{cor:smoothAn}
Every $[A_n]$ is a smooth point of the corresponding algebra-structure scheme.
<!-- end corollary-1 -->
<!-- proof-8: body_md -->
Use Theorem~\ref{thm:main-existence}, Proposition~\ref{prop:center-count} and Lemmas~\ref{lem:h1h2} and \ref{lem:smooth-criterion}.
<!-- end proof-8 -->
<!-- proposition-5: body_md -->
\label{prop:unique-principle}
Let $A$ be a finite-dimensional algebra such that $[A]\in\mathcal M_d$ is smooth.  If $A$ deforms to two semisimple algebras $S$ and $T$, then $S\cong T$.
<!-- end proposition-5 -->
<!-- proof-9: body_md -->
A smooth point lies on a unique irreducible component of $\mathcal M_d$.
Because a semisimple algebra is separable in characteristic zero, $\operatorname{HH}^2(S,S)=0$; hence its orbit is open in $\mathcal M_d$ near $[S]$.  Equivalently, the closure $\overline{O_S}$ is an irreducible component.  The same holds for $T$.
The two deformations give
\[
 [A]\in\overline{O_S}\cap\overline{O_T}.
\]
By uniqueness of the irreducible component through the smooth point, the two orbit closures coincide.  Both $O_S$ and $O_T$ are nonempty open subsets of the same irreducible variety, so they intersect.  Distinct $G$-orbits are disjoint; hence the orbits coincide and $S\cong T$.
<!-- end proof-9 -->
<!-- proof-10: body_md -->
By Corollary~\ref{cor:smoothAn}, $[A_n]$ is smooth.  The semisimple algebra in Theorem~\ref{thm:main-existence} supplies one semisimple deformation.  Apply Proposition~\ref{prop:unique-principle} to any other semisimple target.
<!-- end proof-10 -->
<!-- corollary-2: body_md -->
\label{cor:wemyss}
Wemyss' semisimple-deformation question has an affirmative answer for every contraction algebra in the $E_{6,n}$ family.  The unique semisimple targets are
\[
 \begin{cases}
 \Bbbk^6\times\operatorname{M}_2(\Bbbk)^3\times\operatorname{M}_3(\Bbbk),&n=4,\\
 \Bbbk^7\times\operatorname{M}_2(\Bbbk)^{n-1}\times\operatorname{M}_3(\Bbbk),&n\ge5.
 \end{cases}
\]
Thus the block multiplicities are
\[
 (n_1,n_2,n_3)=
 \begin{cases}
 (6,3,1),&n=4,\\
 (7,n-1,1),&n\ge5.
 \end{cases}
\]
<!-- end corollary-2 -->
<!-- theorem-3: body_md -->
\label{thm:full-p}
For every such $p$, the completed algebra satisfies
\[
 (\dim_\Bbbk A_p,\dim_\Bbbk Z(A_p))=
 \begin{cases}(27,10),&n=4,\\ (4n+12,n+7),&n\ge5.\end{cases}
\]
It admits a finite free one-parameter deformation with geometric
semisimple generic fibre $\Bbbk^6\times\operatorname{M}_2(\Bbbk)^3\times\operatorname{M}_3(\Bbbk)$
for $n=4$, and $\Bbbk^7\times\operatorname{M}_2(\Bbbk)^{n-1}\times\operatorname{M}_3(\Bbbk)$
for $n\ge5$.  This is the unique semisimple flat-deformation target of $A_p$.
Over $\mathbb C$, every such $A_p$ is realized by a smooth
threefold flop as in Corollary~\ref{cor:p-formal-flop-realization}.
<!-- end theorem-3 -->
<!-- theorem-4: body_md -->
\label{ap:thm:subfamily}
Fix \(n\ge4\) and a unit \(h(z)\in\Bbbk[[z]]\). Then
$\operatorname{Jac}\bigl(x^3+xy^3+y^nh(y^3)\bigr)\cong A_n$.
Consequently this entire infinite-parameter subfamily has the same
dimension, centre dimension, and distinguished semisimple deformation
target as \(A_n\).
<!-- end theorem-4 -->
<!-- proof-11: body_md -->
Denote the algebra on the left by \(A_h\), put \(z=y^3\), and set
\[
U(z)=h(z)+\frac3n zh'(z),\qquad
\beta(z)=U(z)^{2/(2n-9)},\qquad \alpha(z)=\beta(z)^{3/2}.
\]
All these are central units in \(A_h\): the relation
\(3x^2+y^3=0\) implies that \(z=-3x^2\) commutes with both \(x\)
and \(y\). The other Jacobi relation is
\(R(x,y)+ny^{n-1}U(z)=0\), where
\(R(x,y)=xy^2+yxy+y^2x\). Put
\(X=\alpha(z)x\) and \(Y=\beta(z)y\). Then
$3X^2+Y^3=\beta^3(3x^2+y^3)=0$,
and, because \(\beta^{n-9/2}=U\),
\[
R(X,Y)+nY^{n-1}
=\beta^{7/2}\bigl(R(x,y)+ny^{n-1}U(z)\bigr)=0.
\]
Thus \(X,Y\) define a homomorphism \(A_n\to A_h\).

For completeness, this is an isomorphism without any appeal to a
dimension comparison. The substitution
\(x\mapsto\alpha(y^3)x\), \(y\mapsto\beta(y^3)y\)
is an automorphism of the completed free algebra: its linear part has
two nonzero diagonal coefficients. In the quotient by the image of the
monomial Jacobi ideal, \(Y^3=-3X^2\) is central. But
\(Y^3=f(y^3)\), where \(f(z)=z\beta(z)^3\) is invertible under
formal composition. Hence \(y^3=f^{-1}(Y^3)\) is also central.
We may therefore reverse the two displayed relation calculations,
recovering exactly the Jacobi ideal of \(A_h\). This proves equality
of the two closed ideals after substitution.
<!-- end proof-11 -->
<!-- lemma-4: body_md -->
\label{ap:lem:jets}
Let \(F=\Bbbk\langle\!\langle x,y\rangle\!\rangle\) with
augmentation ideal \(\mathfrak m\), and let \(I,I'\) be closed ideals
generated by corresponding lists \(r_i,r'_i\). If
\(\mathfrak m^N\subseteq I\) and
\(r_i-r'_i\in\mathfrak m^{N+1}\) for every \(i\), then \(I=I'\).
<!-- end lemma-4 -->
<!-- proof-12: body_md -->
Modulo \(\mathfrak m^{N+1}\) the two quotient algebras agree, and
\(\mathfrak m^N\subseteq I'+\mathfrak m^{N+1}\).
In \(F/I'\), this says \(J^N=J^{N+1}\); iteration and separatedness
of the completed augmentation filtration imply \(J^N=0\).
Therefore \(\mathfrak m^N\subseteq I'\). The differences
\(r_i-r'_i\) now lie in both ideals, giving both inclusions.
<!-- end proof-12 -->
<!-- proposition-6: body_md -->
\label{ap:prop:tails}
Let \(h(0)\ne0\). The conclusion of Theorem~\ref{ap:thm:subfamily}
continues to hold if the potential \(y^nh(y^3)\) is replaced by
\[
y^nh(y^3)+e(y),\quad
\begin{cases}
e(y)\in y^{12}\Bbbk[[y]],&n=4,\\
e(y)\in y^{n+9}\Bbbk[[y]],&n\ge5.
\end{cases}
\]
In particular, the coefficients of these arbitrarily high powers
may be chosen independently and without a smallness condition.
<!-- end proposition-6 -->
<!-- proof-13: body_md -->
Appendix~\ref{app:four} gives \(J(A_4)^{10}=0\), and the
higher-corank sequence of Brown--Wemyss~\cite[\S1.3 and
Definition~4.9]{BW2025} gives
\(J(A_n)^{n+7}=0\) for \(n\ge5\): its listed quotients
\(J^i/J^{i+1}\), together with the total length \(4n+12\), exhaust
the algebra by degree \(n+6\). These are also the nilpotence
bounds for \(A_h\) by Theorem~\ref{ap:thm:subfamily}. The \(y\)-derivative
of \(e(y)\) lies respectively in \(\mathfrak m^{11}\) or
\(\mathfrak m^{n+8}\). Apply Lemma~\ref{ap:lem:jets} with
\(N=10\) or \(N=n+7\).
<!-- end proof-13 -->
<!-- theorem-5: body_md -->
\label{ap:thm:finite}
Let \(p(y)=c_ny^n+O(y^{n+1})\in\Bbbk[[y]]\), where
\(n\ge4\) and \(c_n\ne0\). Then
$\dim_{\Bbbk}A_p<\infty$.
Moreover, for the commutative abelianization,
\[
\dim_{\Bbbk}(A_p)_{\mathrm{ab}}=
\begin{cases}6,&n=4,\\7,&n\ge5.\end{cases}
\]
<!-- end theorem-5 -->
<!-- proof-14: body_md -->
Write \(q(y)=p'(y)\), \(z=y^3=-3x^2\) and \(R=\Bbbk[[z]]\).
The four reduction rules displayed in the next section span
\(A_p\) over \(R\) by
$y^i, y^ix, y^ixy, y^ixyx$ for $0\le i\le2$.
Indeed, they replace \(x^2,y^3,xy^2,xyxy\) by words of smaller
length-lexicographic order \(x>y\), treating their coefficients in
\(R\) as scalars. The twelve words avoiding these four subwords are
exactly the displayed list. Reduction of polynomials, followed by
completeness, gives a surjection \(R^{12}\twoheadrightarrow A_p\):
modulo \(z\), all words of length six vanish, so
\(J(A_p)^6\subseteq zA_p\), ensuring convergence in the
\(z\)-adic topology.
Thus \(B=A_p\otimes_RK\) is an algebra of dimension at most twelve
over \(K=\Bbbk((z))\).

We claim \(B=0\). Otherwise, over an algebraic closure \(L\) of \(K\),
\(B\otimes_K L\) has a simple module \(V\) of dimension at most three:
the square of the dimension of a simple module is bounded by the
dimension of a finite-dimensional algebra. Let \(X,Y\) be the matrices
of \(x,y\) on \(V\). The three roots \(\lambda_i=\omega^i\lambda\) of
\(T^3-z\), with \(\lambda^3=z\), are distinct. Hence \(Y\) is
diagonalizable. On each of its eigenspaces, the diagonal part of the
second Jacobi relation forces the corresponding diagonal block of
\(X\) to be scalar:
\[
X_{ii}=\alpha_i I,\qquad
\alpha_i=-\frac{q(\lambda_i)}{3\lambda_i^2}.
\]
If an eigenspace has dimension at least two, then, since \(\dim V\le3\),
the map from it to the sum of the other eigenspaces under \(X\) has
a nonzero kernel. A line in that kernel is invariant under both
\(X\) and \(Y\), contradicting simplicity unless \(\dim V=1\).
It remains to exclude simple modules with one, two, or three distinct
\(Y\)-eigenvalues.

For a one-dimensional module, \(X^2=-z/3\) and
\(3X\lambda^2+q(\lambda)=0\) give
\(q(\lambda)^2+3\lambda^7=0\). The two summands have different
\(\lambda\)-adic orders \(2n-2\) and \(7\), a contradiction.
For a two-dimensional module with distinct \(Y\)-eigenvalues
\(\lambda_i,\lambda_j\), both off-diagonal entries of \(X\) must be
nonzero for simplicity. The off-diagonal part of \(X^2=-zI/3\)
then forces \(\alpha_i+\alpha_j=0\). But the leading term of this sum
is a nonzero multiple of
\(\lambda_i^{n-3}(1+\omega^{(j-i)(n-3)})\);
\(1+\omega^k\ne0\) for every integer \(k\). Finally, in dimension
three all three \(Y\)-eigenvalues are distinct, and the trace is
\[
\operatorname{tr}X=\sum_{i=0}^2\alpha_i=-c(z),
\qquad q(y)=a(z)+yb(z)+y^2c(z),\quad c(z)\in zR.
\]
Since \(X^2=-zI/3\), its eigenvalues are \(\pm\sqrt{-z/3}\).
In dimension three its trace belongs to
\[
\bigl\{\sqrt{-z/3},-\sqrt{-z/3},
3\sqrt{-z/3},-3\sqrt{-z/3}\bigr\}.
\]
Each possibility has \(z\)-adic order \(1/2\), whereas \(-c(z)\)
is zero or has integral order at least one. Thus \(B=0\).
A finite \(R\)-module that becomes
zero upon inverting \(z\) is annihilated by some power of \(z\),
so \(A_p\) is finite dimensional over \(\Bbbk\).

For the final assertion, abelianization gives
\[
(A_p)_{\mathrm{ab}}
\cong \frac{\Bbbk[[y]][x]}
{(x^2+y^3/3,\;q(y)+3xy^2)}.
\]
The first quotient is free of rank two over \(\Bbbk[[y]]\).
Multiplication by \(q(y)+3xy^2\), in its basis \(1,x\), has
determinant \(q(y)^2+3y^7\). Its cokernel has length equal to the
\(y\)-adic order of this determinant. That order is six when
\(n=4\), and seven when \(n\ge5\).
<!-- end proof-14 -->
<!-- proposition-7: body_md -->
\label{ap:prop:overlap}
In \(A_p=\operatorname{Jac}(x^3+xy^3+p(y))\), the following element is zero:
\begin{align*}
\mathcal R(a,b,c)={}&
 a\left(xyx+\tfrac z3y\right)
 +b\left(yxyx-\tfrac23zy^2\right)
 +c\left(4y^2xyx-\tfrac23z^2\right)\\
 &+b^2yx+b^2cy+abx+abc+ac(xy+yx)+2ac^2y\\
 &+bc(yxy+5y^2x)+3bc^2y^2
   +4c^2(y^2xy+zx)+2c^3z.
\end{align*}
The identity holds for arbitrary formal series \(a,b,c\).
<!-- end proposition-7 -->
<!-- proof-15: body_md -->
Reduce \(xyxxyy\) first using its middle \(x^2\), and then
using its final \(xy^2\). Repeatedly apply the four displayed
rules; the difference of the resulting reduced expressions is
exactly \(\mathcal R(a,b,c)\). This is an identity in the
algebra because both expressions equal \(xyxxyy\). As a consistency
check, setting \((b,c)=(0,0)\), \((a,c)=(0,0)\), or
\((a,b)=(0,0)\) gives respectively \(\rho_0\), \(\rho_1\), or
\(2\rho_2\) from the monomial proof, with the nonzero coefficient
replaced by a central series.
<!-- end proof-15 -->
<!-- theorem-6: body_md -->
\label{ap:thm:alltraces}
Write \(a(z)=zA(z)\), \(b(z)=zB(z)\), \(c(z)=zC(z)\), so
\(q(y)=y^3(A+yB+y^2C)\). In the vector-space cyclic quotient
\(\operatorname{HH}_0(A_p)=A_p/[A_p,A_p]\), the following two classes vanish:
\begin{align*}
F_1={}&\tfrac13A^3y^7+(A+\tfrac12A^2B)y^8
-\tfrac12By^9\\
&-(2C+\tfrac16B^3+ABC)y^{10}
-(B^2C+AC^2)y^{11}
-\tfrac32BC^2y^{12}-\tfrac23C^3y^{13},\\
F_2={}&\tfrac16A^3y^8+\tfrac12Ay^9
-(B+\tfrac12AB^2-A^2C)y^{10}\\
&+(2C-\tfrac13B^3+ABC)y^{11}
+\tfrac32AC^2y^{12}+BC^2y^{13}+\tfrac23C^3y^{14}.
\end{align*}
Here \(A,B,C\) are evaluated at \(z=y^3\); brackets are suppressed
in the display. In particular, at \(p(y)=y^n\) these recover the two
terminal identities
\([y^{n+4}]+\frac{n^2}{3}[y^{3n-5}]=0\) and
\([y^{n+5}]+\frac{n^2}{3}[y^{3n-4}]=0\), after division by
nonzero scalar coefficients.
<!-- end theorem-6 -->
<!-- proof-16: body_md -->
The Jacobi relation, multiplied by \(y^{j-2}\) and rotated, gives
\([y^jx]=-\frac13[y^{j-2}q]\) for \(j\ge2\). Write
\(T_i=[y^ixyx]\). Rotation of the relations multiplied by
\(x\) and \(yx\) gives
\[
T_0=-\tfrac13[y^4],\qquad
T_1=\tfrac23[y^5]+\tfrac13[y^{-2}q^2],\qquad
T_2=\tfrac16[y^6]+\tfrac16[y^{-1}q^2].
\]
The negative powers here are only notation for formal series:
\(q\in y^3\Bbbk[[y]]\), so \(y^{-2}q^2\) and
\(y^{-1}q^2\) are honest power series. Multiply the algebra identity
\(\mathcal R(a,b,c)=0\) by \(y\) and \(y^2\) before passing to
\(\operatorname{HH}_0\). Replace every one-\(x\) term by the first trace rule,
and every two-\(x\) term by the three displayed \(T_i\), using the
centrality of \(z\) to reduce higher indices modulo three. Collecting
coefficients yields precisely \(F_1\) and \(F_2\), respectively.
For example, when \(q=ny^{n-1}\), precisely one of \(A,B,C\)
is nonzero, and the resulting linear and cubic terms give the two
stated monomial formulas; at \(n=4\), these relate \(y^8\) to
\(y^7\) and \(y^9\) to \(y^8\).
<!-- end proof-16 -->
<!-- corollary-3: body_md -->
\label{ap:cor:bound}
For arbitrary \(p\) of order \(n\), if
\(J(A_p)^{10}=0\) when \(n=4\), respectively
\(J(A_p)^{n+7}=0\) when \(n\ge5\), then
\[
\dim\operatorname{HH}_0(A_p)\le
\begin{cases}10,&n=4,\\n+7,&n\ge5.\end{cases}
\]
This assertion does not imply the same bound on \(\dim Z(A_p)\)
without a symmetrizing form.
<!-- end corollary-3 -->
<!-- proof-17: body_md -->
The twelve-word spanning list, rotated cyclically and reduced by the
trace formulas in the preceding proof, shows that \(\operatorname{HH}_0(A_p)\)
is spanned by pure powers of \(y\), \([x]\), and \([xy]\).
The stated nilpotence bounds leave at most ten pure powers for
\(n=4\) and \(n+7\) for \(n\ge5\). The two displayed
relations are linearly independent on these pure-power lists:
at \(n=4\) their lowest nonzero terms have degrees seven and eight,
respectively; for \(n\ge5\) those degrees are \(n+4\) and
\(n+5\). Their coefficients are nonzero multiples of \(c_n\)
(of \(c_4^3\) when \(n=4\)). Subtracting two relations from the
spanning counts, and retaining the two mixed classes, proves the bound.
<!-- end proof-17 -->
<!-- lemma-5: body_md -->
\label{lem:homogeneous-order-quotient}
Let
\[
 C=\frac{\Bbbk\langle\!\langle x,y\rangle\!\rangle}
 {\overline{(x^2+y^3/3,\;xy^2+yxy+y^2x)}},
 \qquad z=y^3.
\]
Use the matrix realization of Theorem~\ref{thm:Ainf-exact}, rescaling
$x$ by a square root of $-1/3$, and write $D=\operatorname{diag}(1,-1)$.
For $N\ge8$, $u^ND$ belongs to $C$ and generates a two-sided ideal.
The homogeneous algebra
\[
 G_N=C/(Cu^ND),\qquad \operatorname{wt}(x)=3,\quad
 \operatorname{wt}(y)=2,\quad \operatorname{wt}(u)=2,
\]
satisfies
\[
 \dim_\Bbbk G_N=4N,\qquad \dim_\Bbbk Z(G_N)=N+4.
\]
<!-- end lemma-5 -->
<!-- proof-18: body_md -->
Put $R_0=\Bbbk[[u^3]]$ and $R=\Bbbk[[u]]$. The twelve-word basis
in Theorem~\ref{thm:Ainf-exact} decomposes into diagonal and
off-diagonal lattices of rank six over $R_0$. Identify the latter
with a lattice of pairs by writing its matrices as
\[
 \begin{pmatrix}0&us\\u^2t&0\end{pmatrix}.
\]
Constant rescaling of $x$ does not change these lattices. With
$\omega^3=1\ne\omega$, they are
\[
\begin{aligned}
 \mathscr D={}&R_0(1,1)+R_0u(\omega,\omega^2)
 +R_0u^2(\omega^2,\omega)\\
 &+R_0u^4(\omega^2,\omega)+R_0u^5(1,1)
 +R_0u^6(\omega,\omega^2),\\
 \mathscr O={}&R_0(1,1)+R_0u(\omega,\omega^2)
 +R_0u(\omega^2,\omega)\\
 &+R_0u^2(\omega^2,\omega)+R_0u^2(1,1)
 +R_0u^3(\omega,\omega^2).
\end{aligned}
\]
These lists follow simply by separating the diagonal words
$y^i,y^ixyx$ from the off-diagonal words $y^ix,y^ixy$.
The matrix grading assigns degrees $1$ and $-1$ to $E_{12}$
and $E_{21}$, respectively; thus the matrix representing $x$
has degree three.
The diagonal lattice contains $u^6R^2$, so $u^ND\in C$.
Conjugation by $D$ fixes $y$ and sends $x$ to $-x$; it preserves
$C$. Hence $Cu^ND=u^NDC$ is a two-sided ideal.

Multiplication by $u^ND$ has determinant valuation $2N$ on each
rank-six lattice over $R_0$: on its two-dimensional fraction-field
extension this is the norm of the determinant $-u^{2N}$.
Consequently the diagonal and off-diagonal quotients each have
length $2N$, giving $\dim G_N=4N$.

We calculate the centre using the two generators $x,y$. Write
$\delta(s,t)=s-t$. The displayed lattices give
\[
\begin{gathered}
 \mathscr D\cap\Bbbk((u))(1,1)
   =\Bbbk[[u^3,u^4,u^5]](1,1),\\
 \delta\mathscr D=\Bbbk u+\Bbbk u^2+u^4R,\qquad
 \mathscr O\cap\Bbbk((u))(1,1)=R(1,1),\\
 uD\mathscr O\subseteq\mathscr O,\qquad
 u^2\delta\mathscr O\subseteq\Bbbk[[u^3,u^4,u^5]].
\end{gathered}
\]
For a diagonal class, commutation with $x$ modulo the ideal is
equivalent to $\delta\in u^NR$; commutation with $y$ is automatic.
Its central subspace therefore has dimension
\[
 2N-\dim_\Bbbk(\delta\mathscr D/u^NR)
 =2N-(N-2)=N+2.
\]
For an off-diagonal class, commutation with $y$ is equivalent to
membership in $u^{N-1}\mathscr O$. Commutation with $x$ then
follows from the last inclusion in the display. The quotient
\[
 u^{N-1}\mathscr O/u^ND\mathscr O
 \cong\mathscr O/uD\mathscr O
\]
has dimension two, again by the determinant norm. The two parts
are independent, and their dimensions sum to $N+4$.
<!-- end proof-18 -->
<!-- lemma-6: body_md -->
\label{lem:weighted-upper-bound}
If $\operatorname{ord}p=n\ge5$, then
$\dim A_p\le4n+12$.
If equality holds, the filtration with weights $3,2$ on $x,y$
has associated graded algebra $G_{n+3}$. In particular
$\dim Z(A_p)\le n+7$.
<!-- end lemma-6 -->
<!-- proof-19: body_md -->
Write $n-1=3q+r$, $0\le r\le2$. The initial Jacobi relations
are those of $C$, since $p'(y)$ has weight at least eight.
The initial form of the overlap in  Proposition~\ref{ap:prop:overlap} is
\[
 nc_nz^qE_r,\qquad
 E_0=xyx+zy/3,\quad E_1=yxyx-2zy^2/3,\quad
 E_2=4y^2xyx-2z^2/3.
\]
Terms quadratic in the coefficients have larger weight: the
weight increase is at least $2n-9>0$. Higher coefficients also
have strictly larger weight. In the generic matrix realization,
each $E_r$ is a nonzero scalar multiple of $u^{4+r}D$.
For example their squares are respectively
$-u^8/3,-u^{10}/3,-4u^{12}/3$.
Thus the initial ideal contains $Cu^{n+3}D$, and there is a
graded surjection $G_{n+3}\twoheadrightarrow\operatorname{gr}A_p$.
The preceding lemma gives the length bound. Equality makes this
surjection an isomorphism; the filtered centre inclusion then
gives the centre bound.
<!-- end proof-19 -->
<!-- lemma-7: body_md -->
\label{lem:order-four-upper-bound}
If $\operatorname{ord}p=4$, then
$\dim A_p\le27, J(A_p)^{10}=0$.
<!-- end lemma-7 -->
<!-- proof-20: body_md -->
Write $p'(y)=y^3U(y)$, $U(0)=A=4c_4\ne0$, and use the ordinary
augmentation filtration. The initial relations, ordered
lexicographically with $x>y$ within each degree, include
\[
\begin{gathered}
 x^2=0,\qquad xy^2=-yxy-y^2x-Ay^3,\qquad
 xyxy=yxyx,\qquad y^3xyx=0,\\
 y^6xy=y^7x,\qquad y^8x=-Ay^9/3,\qquad y^{10}=0.
\end{gathered}
\]
Here the first three follow from the Jacobi relations and their
commutator. The overlap of Proposition~\ref{ap:prop:overlap} gives
$y^3xyx\in J^7$. Its commutator with $x$, before taking initial
forms, gives $y^6xy-y^7x\in J^9$; the coefficient of this term
is $2A/3$. The term $abx$ commutes with $x$, and every other
correction has order at least nine, so none changes this initial
relation. Multiplying the second Jacobi relation by $y^6$ now gives
$3y^8x+Ay^9\in J^{10}$.
Multiplication by $x$, using $x^2=-y^3/3$, yields
$Ay^9x\in J^{11}$; multiplication by $y$ yields
$3y^9x+Ay^{10}\in J^{11}$. Since $A\ne0$, these imply
$y^{10}\in J^{11}$, as asserted.

The seven homogeneous rules lower lexicographic order. The words
avoiding their left sides have degree counts
\[
 1,2,3,4,4,4,3,3,2,1\qquad(0\le d\le9),
\]
and there are no such words in higher degree. This proves a
graded spanning bound of $27$; confluence is not needed.
Moreover $J^{10}=J^{11}$, and separatedness of the completed
augmentation filtration implies $J^{10}=0$.
<!-- end proof-20 -->
<!-- theorem-7: body_md -->
\label{ap:thm:all-parameters}
For every \(p(y)=c_ny^n+O(y^{n+1})\) with \(c_n\ne0\),
\[
\bigl(\dim_{\Bbbk} A_p,\dim_{\Bbbk} Z(A_p)\bigr)
=\begin{cases}(27,10),&n=4,\\(4n+12,n+7),&n\ge5.
\end{cases}
\]
These formulas hold even when the parameters in different
\(y\bmod3\) residues vary independently.
<!-- end theorem-7 -->
<!-- proof-21: body_md -->
Theorem~\ref{ap:thm:finite} gives finite length.
The generic split semisimple quotient construction for the
formal deformation
\begin{equation}\label{ap:eq:deformation}
 \mathcal A_p=\operatorname{Jac}_{\Bbbk[[t]]}
 \bigl(x^3+xy^3+p(y)+ty^3/3-b_0t^2y\bigr),\qquad
 b_0=\begin{cases}c_4,&n=4,\\c_5^{-1},&n=5,\\1,&n\ge6,
 \end{cases}
\end{equation}
produces, after a Puiseux extension, a quotient of dimension
\(d=27\) or \(d=4n+12\), of block type \(S_4\) or \(S_n\)
from Theorem~\ref{thm:main-existence}. We give the construction to make the lower bound
independent of the filtered upper bounds. Put
\(Q(y)=p'(y)+ty^2-b_0t^2\). Scalar representations are the
simple roots of \(Q(y)^2+3y^7=0\), with \(x=-Q(y)/(3y^2)\).
For \(n\ge5\), the edge \(y=t^{4/7}u\) gives the seven roots
of \(b_0^2+3u^7\). For \(n=4\), set \(t=s^3\) and
\(y=s^2(u+sv)\); the three nonzero values \(u^3=1/4\)
each give two simple roots through
\((12c_4u^2v+u^2)^2+3u^7=0\). Thus the scalar-block counts
are seven and six, respectively.

For two-dimensional representations choose a root \(\lambda\ne0\)
of
\begin{equation}\label{ap:eq:generic-two}
 p'(\lambda)+\omega p'(\omega\lambda)
 +2t\lambda^2-(1+\omega)b_0t^2=0,
\end{equation}
where \(\omega^3=1\ne\omega\), put
\(a_\lambda=-Q(\lambda)/(3\lambda^2)\), and choose
\(\beta_\lambda^2=-\lambda^3/3-a_\lambda^2\). Then
\[
 Y_\lambda=\operatorname{diag}(\lambda,\omega\lambda),\qquad
 X_\lambda=
 \begin{pmatrix}a_\lambda&\beta_\lambda\\
 \beta_\lambda&-a_\lambda\end{pmatrix}
\]
satisfy both Jacobi relations. At \(n=4\), equation
\eqref{ap:eq:generic-two} has three simple roots with
\(\lambda=t^{2/3}u+O(t)\), \(u^3=1/4\), and
\(\beta_\lambda^2=t^2/4+o(t^2)\). At \(n=5\), writing
\(\lambda=t^{1/2}u\) produces
\(-5c_5\omega u^4+2u^2+b_0\omega^2\), whose discriminant
as a polynomial in \(u^2\) is
\(4+20b_0c_5=24\). For \(n\ge6\), two roots have valuation
\(1/2\), and \(n-3\) roots have valuation \(1/(n-3)\):
their nonzero leading equations are respectively
\(2u^2=(1+\omega)b_0\) and
\(nc_n(1+\omega^n)u^{n-3}+2=0\).
For \(n\ge5\), \(a_\lambda^2\) has strictly greater
valuation than \(\lambda^3\); hence every \(\beta_\lambda\ne0\).
This gives \(n-1\) pairwise distinct irreducible two-dimensional
representations (three at \(n=4\)).

For the remaining block, define
$r(t,h)=t+\sum_{\substack{m\ge n\\3\mid m}}
 m c_m h^{(m-3)/3}$.
The implicit equation \(h+3r(t,h)^2=0\) has a solution
\(h=-3t^2+O(t^3)\). Let \(\lambda_i=\omega^i\lambda\)
with \(\lambda^3=h\), put
\(a_i=-Q(\lambda_i)/(3\lambda_i^2)\), \(v_i=a_i+r(t,h)\),
and set
\[
 Y=\operatorname{diag}(\lambda_0,\lambda_1,\lambda_2),
 \qquad X=\mathbf1(v_0,v_1,v_2)-r(t,h)I_3.
\]
The root-of-unity sum gives \(\sum_i a_i=-r(t,h)\), so
\(X^2=r(t,h)^2I_3=-hI_3/3\). Its diagonal entries are
\(a_i\), and all off-diagonal terms of the other Jacobi relation
vanish since \(\lambda_i^3=h\). Each \(v_i\ne0\) by its
leading \(t\)-valuation; thus this three-dimensional representation
is irreducible. All blocks have different dimensions or distinct
\(Y\)-spectra. The irreducible representation maps jointly
surject onto the claimed product of matrix algebras.

Since $A_p$ is finite dimensional, Lemma~\ref{lem:topNak} applies to
$\mathcal A_p$. The generic quotient gives $\dim A_p\ge d$.
The reverse inequality follows from Lemmas 
\ref{lem:weighted-upper-bound} and \ref{lem:order-four-upper-bound}.
Thus $\dim A_p=d$, and Lemma~\ref{lem:topNak} shows that the
deformation is finite free and its generic quotient is the whole fibre.

For $n\ge5$, Lemma~\ref{lem:weighted-upper-bound} gives
$\dim Z(A_p)\le n+7$. Kernel dimension for the commutator map
cannot decrease under specialization of a finite free algebra,
so its generic centre gives the reverse inequality.

For $n=4$, Lemma~\ref{lem:order-four-upper-bound} and Theorem~\ref{ap:thm:alltraces}
give $\dim\operatorname{HH}_0(A_p)\le10$: the twelve-word cyclic spanning
list has ten pure-power classes and $[x],[xy]$, and the two
trace relations eliminate distinct lowest degrees seven and eight.
Flat specialization from the ten generic blocks gives equality.
Over $\mathbb C$, the geometric realization proved independently
in Corollary~\ref{cor:p-formal-flop-realization} makes $A_p$ symmetric;
therefore $\dim Z(A_p)=\dim\operatorname{HH}_0(A_p)=10$.
The same conclusion holds over any algebraically closed field
of characteristic zero. Indeed all relations are determined by
a finite jet, by Lemma~\ref{ap:lem:jets}; its finitely many coefficients
lie in a finitely generated characteristic-zero field, which
embeds into $\mathbb C$. Lengths and the kernels of the
commutator matrices are unchanged by field extension.
<!-- end proof-21 -->
<!-- corollary-4: body_md -->
\label{cor:parameter-rank}
For any $p$ in \cref{thm:full-p}, let
$\Gamma_p(a)=([x,a],[y,a])$. Then
\[
\operatorname{rank}\Gamma_p=
\begin{cases}17,&\operatorname{ord}_yp=4,\\
3n+5,&\operatorname{ord}_yp=n\ge5.
\end{cases}
\]
Consequently, for series $p_n,p_{n+1}$ of orders $n,n+1$
with $n\ge5$, respectively,
\[
\operatorname{rank}\Gamma_{p_{n+1}}-\operatorname{rank}\Gamma_{p_n}=3.
\]
<!-- end corollary-4 -->
<!-- proof-22: body_md -->
The kernel of $\Gamma_p$ is $Z(A_p)$. Subtract the centre
dimension in \cref{ap:thm:all-parameters} from the algebra length.
<!-- end proof-22 -->
<!-- remark-3: body_md -->
Theorem~\ref{ap:thm:all-parameters} proves the all-parameter length,
centre, and flatness assertions for this \(E_{6,n}\) family.
It does not classify isomorphism types among parameters: general
\(y^4+\eta y^5+\theta y^6\) potentials have genuine moduli
\cite[Section~5.1]{BW2025}. The algebraic equality
$\dim\operatorname{HH}^1(A_p)=\dim\operatorname{HH}^2(A_p)$ is sufficient for uniqueness by
Lemma~\ref{lem:smooth-criterion} and Proposition~\ref{prop:unique-principle}. Over $\mathbb C$,
Theorem~\ref{thm:p-projective-contraction} and a sufficiently long polynomial
truncation realize every such $A_p$ as a smooth-flop contraction
algebra, providing this Hochschild equality.
The finite \(E_7,E_{8,5},E_{8,6}\) cases do not follow from this
two-generator calculation; they are treated via their universal
flopping algebras in the companion universal-flop manuscript.
<!-- end remark-3 -->
<!-- proof-23: body_md -->
The original-algebra length and centre identities and the finite
free deformation are Theorem~\ref{ap:thm:all-parameters}.
The centre dimension equals that of the semisimple generic fibre.
Over $\mathbb C$, Corollary~\ref{cor:p-formal-flop-realization} and Lemma~\ref{lem:h1h2}
give $h^1(A_p)=h^2(A_p)$. Thus Lemma~\ref{lem:smooth-criterion}
proves smoothness, and Proposition~\ref{prop:unique-principle} proves uniqueness.
For an arbitrary algebraically closed characteristic-zero field,
replace $p$ by a finite jet using Lemma~\ref{ap:lem:jets}, descend its
coefficients to a finitely generated field, and embed that field
into $\mathbb C$. The finite-dimensional Hochschild cochain
spaces in each degree commute with field extension, so the same
Hochschild dimension equality holds. The two cited lemmas then
apply over the original field.
<!-- end proof-23 -->
<!-- proposition-8: body_md -->
\label{prop:p-geometric-neighbourhood}
Glue
$U_a=\operatorname{Spec}\mathbb C[a,v_2,v_1],\qquad
 U_b=\operatorname{Spec}\mathbb C[b,w_2,w_1]$
on $a,b\ne0$ by
\begin{equation}\label{eq:p-curve-glue}
 b=a^{-1},\qquad w_2=a^{-1}v_2,\qquad
 w_1=a^3v_1+3a^2v_2^2+a^{-1}v_2^3
       +\sum_{m=n}^{N}m c_m a^{2-m}v_2^{m-1}.
\end{equation}
The resulting $X_P$ is a smooth separated threefold containing the
closed curve $C=\{v_1=v_2=0\}\cong\mathbb P^1$, with
$N_{C/X_P}\cong\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^1}(1)\oplus
\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^1}(-3)$.  Its one-pointed NC deformation
algebra is
\[
 \Lambda_{\mathrm{def}}(\mathcal O_C\subset X_P)
 \cong \operatorname{Jac}(x^3+xy^3+P(y))
 \cong A_p.
\]
The projective local contraction of this curve neighbourhood is proved
in \cref{thm:p-projective-contraction} below.
<!-- end proposition-8 -->
<!-- proof-24: body_md -->
The inverse change of coordinates has
$a=b^{-1}$, $v_2=b^{-1}w_2$ and
\[
 v_1=b^3w_1-3b^{-1}w_2^2-bw_2^3
       -b^2\sum_{m=n}^{N}m c_m w_2^{m-1}.
\]
These formulas are regular on the overlap and show that the charts
glue by an isomorphism.  Smoothness follows from the two affine charts;
the separatedness of precisely this gluing is
\cite[Lemma~2.2]{BWCrepant2024}.  Along $C$ all nonlinear terms
vanish, and the linear transitions are $w_1=a^3v_1$ and
$w_2=a^{-1}v_2$, giving the asserted normal bundle.

In the notation of \cite[Corollary~1.2]{BWCrepant2024}, set
\[
 \lambda_{3,0}=3,\qquad \lambda_{1,3}=1,\qquad
 \lambda_{0,m}=m c_m\ (n\le m\le N),
\]
and set all other gluing coefficients to zero.  The corresponding
free necklace polynomials are
$N_{3,0}=x^3/3$, $N_{1,3}=xy^3$, and
$N_{0,m}=y^m/m$.  Their weighted sum is exactly
$x^3+xy^3+P(y)$, so that corollary identifies the NC deformation
algebra with its completed Jacobi algebra. Tensoring by the invertible
sheaf $\pi^*\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^1}(-1)$, where
$\pi:X_P\to\mathbb P^1$ is the chart projection, identifies the
NC deformation problems of $\mathcal O_C$ and $\mathcal O_C(-1)$.
Thus the usual contraction-algebra convention gives the same algebra
once the local contraction is constructed. The last isomorphism is
the finite-truncation assertion of Lemma~\ref{lem:poly-realization}.
<!-- end proof-24 -->
<!-- proposition-9: body_md -->
\label{prop:p-extra-sections}
For every polynomial $P$ in \eqref{eq:p-curve-glue},
$u=av_1+3v_2^2=b^2w_1-w_2^3-bP'(w_2)$
is a global regular function on $X_P$ and vanishes on $C$.
The sections of the projection $X_P\to\mathbb P^1$ are in bijection
with the critical points $(s,t)$ of the \emph{commutative} polynomial
$F(s,t)=s^3+st^3+P(t)$. The corresponding section
$C_{s,t}\cong\mathbb P^1$ is given on $U_a$ by
\[
 v_2=s+at,\qquad v_1=-6st-3at^2.
\]
Along this section, $u=3s^2=-t^3$.
In particular, already for $P(y)=y^4$, the point
$(s,t)=(64/9,-16/3)$ gives a complete curve $C_{s,t}$
distinct from $C$. Hence there is \emph{no} morphism from this
entire $X_P$ to an affine scheme that contracts exactly $C$.
<!-- end proposition-9 -->
<!-- proof-25: body_md -->
Substituting the inverse transition in \eqref{eq:p-curve-glue}
gives the stated expression for $u$ in the $b$-chart.
Conversely, a section must have $v_2=s+at$: regularity of both
$v_2$ and $w_2=a^{-1}v_2$ forces this form. The only powers of
$a$ at least three in the remaining transition are $6st a^3$
and $3t^2 a^4$, so regularity of $w_1$ forces
$v_1=-6st-3at^2$. On this prospective section, the $b$-chart coordinate
$w_2=bs+t$ is regular.  Substitution into the transition for $w_1$
gives a Laurent polynomial in $a$, whose only positive powers are
$a^2(3s^2+t^3)+a\bigl(3st^2+P'(t)\bigr)$.
Both coefficients vanish precisely when $(s,t)$ is critical for $F$.
The remaining Laurent polynomial is regular in $b=a^{-1}$, so the
two charts glue to a section.  Substitution into $u$ gives $3s^2$;
the first critical equation identifies this with $-t^3$.
For $P(y)=y^4$, direct substitution verifies the displayed critical
point and $u|_{C_{s,t}}=4096/27\ne0=u|_C$.  Every morphism from a
complete connected curve to an affine scheme is constant. Thus a map
from all of $X_P$ to an affine scheme necessarily contracts this
second curve as well.
<!-- end proof-25 -->
<!-- corollary-5: body_md -->
\label{cor:p-isolate-sections}
Suppose $P(y)=c_ny^n+O(y^{n+1})$ is a polynomial, $c_n\ne0$,
$n\ge4$. Define
\[
 D_P(t)=P'(t)^2+3t^7,
 \qquad G_P(U)=\prod_{\substack{t\ne0\\D_P(t)=0}}(U+t^3),
\]
with each distinct root $t$ appearing once. Then $G_P(0)\ne0$,
and the open neighbourhood $X_P^\circ=\{G_P(u)\ne0\}\subseteq X_P$
contains $C$ but no other section of $X_P\to\mathbb P^1$.
This statement does not rule out compact multisections or establish
properness of a morphism from $X_P^\circ$.
<!-- end corollary-5 -->
<!-- proof-26: body_md -->
At $t=0$, the critical equations give $s=0$. At $t\ne0$ they
give $s=-P'(t)/(3t^2)$ and $D_P(t)=0$. The polynomial $D_P$ is
nonzero: it has order $6$ at zero if $n=4$, and order $7$ if
$n\ge5$. Thus there are finitely many other sections, all with
$u=-t^3\ne0$. The indicated localization removes each of them
and retains $C$, since $u|_C=0$.
For the monomials $P=t^n$, one has
$D_P=t^6(16+3t)$ if $n=4$, and
$D_P=t^7(n^2t^{2n-9}+3)$ if $n\ge5$; thus every full
monomial two-chart model has extra sections before localization.
<!-- end proof-26 -->
<!-- proposition-10: body_md -->
\label{prop:p-zero-fibre-curves}
Assume $P\in y^4\mathbb C[y]$. Every complete integral curve
$D\subseteq X_P$ with $u|_D=0$ equals $C$. In particular this holds
inside $X_P^\circ$, independently of the other critical sections.
Moreover, $C$ meets no other complete integral curve in $X_P$.
<!-- end proposition-10 -->
<!-- proof-27: body_md -->
The projection $\pi:X_P\to\mathbb P^1$ has affine-plane fibres.
Thus $\pi|_D$ is nonconstant. On the normalization $B$ of $D$, the
induced map $f:B\to\mathbb P^1$ is finite of some degree $d>0$.
The coordinates $v_2$ and $w_2=a^{-1}v_2$ give a section
$\sigma$ of $L=f^*\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^1}(1)$, with $\deg L=d$.
If $\sigma$ vanishes identically, then $av_1=u-3v_2^2=0$
on the dense open $a\ne0$, and hence $D=C$.

Suppose instead that $\sigma$ is nonzero. Let $q\in f^{-1}(a=0)$
have ramification index $e_q$, and let $k_q$ be the vanishing order
of $v_2$ at $q$. The identity $av_1=-3v_2^2$ implies
$2k_q\ge e_q$. Since the indices over $a=0$ sum to $d$, the
zeros of $\sigma$ there have total degree at least $d/2$.
At $q\in f^{-1}(b=0)$, write $e_q=\operatorname{ord}_q(b)$ and
$k_q=\operatorname{ord}_q(w_2)$. The $b$-chart identity is
\[
 b^2w_1=w_2^3+bP'(w_2).
\]
It first shows $k_q>0$. Since $P'\in y^3\mathbb C[y]$, the
second term on the right has order at least $e_q+3k_q$, strictly
greater than the order $3k_q$ of the first. Therefore
$3k_q\ge2e_q$, and these zeros have total degree at least $2d/3$.
The two collections lie over distinct points of $\mathbb P^1$.
They give more than $d/2+2d/3>d=\deg L$ zeros of a nonzero
section of $L$, a contradiction.
Finally, a regular function is constant on every complete integral
curve. A complete integral curve meeting $C$ has $u=0$ and hence
equals $C$ by the first assertion.
<!-- end proof-27 -->
<!-- proposition-11: body_md -->
\label{prop:p-double-section}
For $P(y)=y^4+y^5$, the open neighbourhood $X_P^\circ$ of
\cref{cor:p-isolate-sections} contains a complete integral curve
$D\ne C$ whose projection to $\mathbb P^1$ has degree two. The
global function $u$ is constant on $D$ with value $64/125$.
Consequently, no morphism from all of $X_P^\circ$ to an affine
scheme contracts only $C$.
<!-- end proposition-11 -->
<!-- proof-28: body_md -->
Put
$k=-\frac45, c=-k^3=\frac{64}{125},
 \ell=5k^3=-\frac{64}{25}$.
On the $a$-chart of the total space of $\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^1}(1)$,
take the monic quadratic curve
\begin{equation}\label{eq:p-double-qa}
 q_a=v_2^2+ka v_2+k^2a^2+\ell a-\frac c3=0,
 \qquad v_1=3kv_2+3k^2a+3\ell.
\end{equation}
On the $b$-chart, multiplying $q_a$ by $b^2$ gives
\[
 q_b=w_2^2+kw_2+k^2+\ell b-\frac c3b^2=0.
\]
Write $w=w_2$, $q_0=w^2+kw+k^2$, and observe that
$P'(w)=w^3(4+5w)=5w^3(w-k)$ and
$w^3-k^3=(w-k)q_0$. In the quotient by $q_b$, where
$q_0=-\ell b+(c/3)b^2$, two substitutions give
\[
 c+w^3+bP'(w)=b^2\left[-5\ell(w-k)^2
   +\frac c3(w-k)+\frac{5c}{3}b(w-k)^2\right].
\]
Thus the bracket defines a regular $w_1$ on the $b$-chart.
The identity $av_1+3v_2^2=c$, obtained from \eqref{eq:p-double-qa},
and the displayed $b$-chart identity show that these two curves
glue inside $X_P$. Since $q_a$ and $q_b$ are monic quadratics,
the resulting curve is finite over $\mathbb P^1$ of degree two,
and hence complete. Its discriminant as a quadratic in $v_2$ is
$-3k^2a^2-4\ell a+4c/3$; this polynomial has two distinct roots
because its discriminant is $16(\ell^2-k^5)\ne0$.
Therefore the double section is integral. The equations give
$u|_D=c\ne0$.

It remains to check that the localization in
Corollary~\ref{cor:p-isolate-sections} does not remove $D$. Its nonzero
critical section parameters are roots of
$25t^2+43t+16=0$. If such a root satisfied $-t^3=c$,
reducing $t^3+64/125$ modulo this quadratic would give
$(1449t+1008)/625=0$, hence $t=-16/23$; however the quadratic
has value $-960/529$ there. Thus $G_P(c)\ne0$ and
$D\subset X_P^\circ$. Every morphism from the complete curve
$D$ to an affine scheme is constant, proving the last assertion.
<!-- end proof-28 -->
<!-- remark-4: body_md -->
Let $\omega^3=1\ne\omega$ and $k\ne0$. The condition
\[
 \Phi_P(k):=P'(\omega k)+\omega P'(\omega^2k)=0
\]
is equivalent to the existence of $\ell\in\mathbb C$ such that
$P'(w)\equiv\ell(w-k)\pmod{w^2+kw+k^2}$.
Set $c=-k^3$ and use \eqref{eq:p-double-qa} with these $k,c,\ell$.
If $H(w)=(P'(w)-\ell(w-k))/(w^2+kw+k^2)$, the same gluing
calculation defines the regular coordinate
\[
 w_1=-\ell H(w_2)+\frac c3(w_2-k)
        +\frac c3bH(w_2).
\]
When $\ell^2\ne k^5$, the quadratic discriminant has distinct
roots, giving a complete integral double section with $u=-k^3$.
For a polynomial $P$ of order $n\ge4$, $\Phi_P$ is nonzero:
its first coefficient is
$n c_n\omega^{n-1}(1+\omega^n)k^{n-1}$.
This describes a finite explicit set of \emph{candidate} values
for these double sections; it does not classify all compact curves.
<!-- end remark-4 -->
<!-- proposition-12: body_md -->
\label{prop:p-all-double-sections}
Let $0\ne P\in y^4\mathbb C[y]$, and let $D\subset X_P$ be a complete
integral curve for which $\pi|_D:D\to\mathbb P^1$ has degree two.
Then $u|_D=c\ne0$.  There is a nonzero root $k$ of
$\Phi_P(k)=P'(\omega k)+\omega P'(\omega^2k)$, uniquely determined
by $D$, such that $c=-k^3$.  Write $\ell$ for the unique scalar with
\[
 P'(w)\equiv\ell(w-k)\pmod{w^2+kw+k^2}.
\]
Then $D$ is exactly the double section of
\eqref{eq:p-double-qa}.  It is integral precisely when
$\ell^2\ne k^5$.  Conversely, each nonzero root $k$ satisfying
$\ell^2\ne k^5$ produces such an integral curve.
Consequently there are only finitely many complete integral curves
of projection degree at most two in $X_P$ besides $C$.  They can all
be removed by a principal open neighbourhood of $C$.
<!-- end proposition-12 -->
<!-- proof-29: body_md -->
The degree-one curves are classified by
Proposition~\ref{prop:p-extra-sections}; $u=0$ contains only $C$ by
Proposition~\ref{prop:p-zero-fibre-curves}.  Consider a degree-two curve with
$u=c\ne0$.  The morphism $D\to\mathbb P^1$ is finite: a fibre is
contained in an affine plane and cannot contain a complete curve.
Since $D$ is integral, $\pi_*\mathcal O_D$ is torsion-free of rank two
and hence locally free.  Multiplication by the restriction of $v_2$,
viewed as a section of $\pi^*\mathcal O(1)$, has a characteristic
equation on the $a$-chart
\[
 q_a=v_2^2+A(a)v_2+B(a)=0,
 \qquad \deg A\le1,\quad\deg B\le2.
\]
If $v_2$ were scalar in the generic quadratic function field,
$av_1=c-3v_2^2$ would make that function field rational over
$\mathbb C(a)$, contradicting the degree.  The same argument works
on the fibre $a=0$: if $v_2=s$ in $\mathcal O_D/a\mathcal O_D$,
then $(v_2-s)/a$ extends regularly to $D$, since on the $b$-chart it
equals $w_2-sb$.  A regular function on the complete integral curve
$D$ is constant, whence $v_2=s+at$ and again the function-field
degree is one.  Thus $v_2$ generates the two-dimensional algebra
$\mathcal O_D/a\mathcal O_D$.  Reducing $av_1=c-3v_2^2$ modulo $a$
now shows that $q_a|_{a=0}=v_2^2-c/3$.  Hence
\[
 A(a)=ka,\qquad B(a)=-c/3+\ell a+h a^2.
\]
In the quotient by $q_a$, the identity $av_1=c-3v_2^2$
gives $v_1=3kv_2+3\ell+3ha$; cancellation of $a$ is valid since
$\mathcal O_D$ is torsion-free over $\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^1}$.

On the $b$-chart the characteristic equation is
$q_b=w_2^2+kw_2+h+\ell b-(c/3)b^2=0$.
If $w_2$ were scalar on the fibre $b=0$, then
$(w_2-s)/b=v_2-sa$ would be a constant regular function on $D$,
again contradicting degree two.  Therefore $w_2$ generates that
fibre algebra.  Reducing
$b^2w_1=c+w_2^3+bP'(w_2)$ modulo $b$ shows that
$w^2+kw+h$ divides $w^3+c$.  As $c\ne0$, the latter has three
distinct roots, and its monic quadratic factors have the form
$w^2+kw+k^2$ with $k^3=-c$.  Thus $h=k^2$.
Write $q_0=w^2+kw+k^2$; since $w^3+c=(w-k)q_0$, the relation
$q_b=0$ gives, modulo $b^2$,
\[
 c+w^3+bP'(w)
 \equiv b\bigl(P'(w)-\ell(w-k)\bigr)
 \pmod{(q_b,b^2)}.
\]
The left-hand side is divisible by $b^2$ in $\mathcal O_D$.
As $w_2$ generates the fibre at $b=0$, it follows that
$P'(w)\equiv\ell(w-k)\pmod{q_0}$.  Evaluation at $\omega k$ and
$\omega^2k$ makes this condition equivalent to $\Phi_P(k)=0$.
{
To justify generation over the whole charts, fix any
$a_0\in\mathbb C$.  If $v_2$ were scalar, say $s$, in the fibre of
$D\to\mathbb P^1$ over $a_0$, then
$(v_2-s)/(a-a_0)$ would be regular on the $a$-chart of $D$.
On the $b$-chart its expression is
$(w_2-sb)/(1-a_0b)$, which is regular at $b=0$; hence it is a
global regular function on the complete integral curve $D$, and
therefore constant.  The identities for $u$ and $v_1$ would then
make the function field of $D$ equal to $\mathbb C(a)$, a
contradiction.  Thus $1,v_2$ generate every finite $a$-fibre;
fibrewise Nakayama makes them a basis of the rank-two algebra on
the whole $a$-chart.  The identical argument with
$(w_2-s)/(b-b_0)=(v_2-sa)/(1-b_0a)$ treats every finite $b$-fibre.
The two monic quadratic charts therefore exhaust $D$ scheme
theoretically, with no additional curve hidden at either end.
}
Near $a=0$ the algebra of $D$ is generated by $v_2$, and the formula
for $v_1$ extends that equality across the whole $a$-chart; the
same holds on the $b$-chart using the displayed formula for $w_1$
in the preceding remark.  Thus the equations identify $D$ with
\eqref{eq:p-double-qa}.  Its quadratic discriminant is
$-3k^2a^2-4\ell a+4c/3$, which is a square in $\mathbb C(a)$
exactly when $\ell^2=k^5$.  The converse construction and
integrality follow from the preceding remark and
\cref{prop:p-double-section}.

Finally $\Phi_P$ is not identically zero: its first nonzero
coefficient is $nc_n\omega^{n-1}(1+\omega^n)k^{n-1}$ if
$P=c_ny^n+O(y^{n+1})$.  Let $G_P(U)$ be as in
\cref{cor:p-isolate-sections} and put
\[
 H_P(U)=G_P(U)
 \prod_{\substack{k\ne0,\ \Phi_P(k)=0}}(U+k^3),
\]
listing each distinct factor once.  Then $H_P(0)\ne0$, and
$\{H_P(u)\ne0\}$ contains $C$ but no other complete integral
curve whose projection has degree at most two.
<!-- end proof-29 -->
<!-- remark-5: body_md -->
\label{rem:contractibility-gate}
The full two-chart threefold can contain complete curves besides
$C$, as Propositons~\ref{prop:p-extra-sections} and \ref{prop:p-double-section} show.
The projective affinization in Theorem~\ref{thm:p-projective-contraction}
may contract those curves to other target points.  A principal
neighbourhood of the distinguished target point removes them.
The valuation argument in Proposition~\ref{prop:p-zero-fibre-curves} excludes
every additional complete curve \emph{over $u=0$}.  The global
function in Proposition~\ref{prop:p-global-boundary-coordinate} rules out
projection degrees greater than three and confines degree-three
curves to finitely many nonzero values of $u$.
\Cref{cor:p-isolate-all-curves} consequently gives a principal
neighbourhood of $C$ with no other complete integral curves.
The explicit properness argument in
\Cref{thm:p-projective-contraction} closes this gate for every
nonzero polynomial $P$ of order at least four.  It uses the
global functions $u,F_P,\mathcal G_P$
and their monic chart equations; finiteness of the NC deformation
algebra alone is not used as a contractibility criterion.
<!-- end remark-5 -->
<!-- proposition-13: body_md -->
\label{prop:p-global-boundary-coordinate}
Let $P\in y^4\mathbb C[y]$, and write
$Q(w)=P'(w)=\sum_{d\ge3}q_dw^d$.  With the global function $u$ of
\Cref{prop:p-extra-sections}, define polynomials on the $a$-chart
\[
 T_{3k}=(-1)^k a u^k,\qquad
 T_{3k+1}=(-1)^k v_2u^k,\qquad
 T_{3k+2}=\frac{(-1)^{k+1}}3v_1u^k
 \quad(k\ge1),
\]
and put
\begin{equation}\label{eq:p-global-boundary-function}
 F_P=a^2u-\frac13v_1v_2+\sum_{d\ge3}q_dT_d.
\end{equation}
Then $F_P$ extends to a global regular function on $X_P$.  On the
affine plane $B=\{b=0\}\subset U_b$, with coordinate $w=w_2$,
\[
 u|_B=-w^3,\qquad F_P|_B=w_1+\Theta_P(w),
\quad
\Theta_P(w)=\frac13w^4+Q(w)
 \sum_{d\ge3}\left\lfloor\frac d3\right\rfloor q_dw^{d-3}.
\]
Consequently $(u,F_P)|_B:B\to\mathbb A^2$ is finite flat of
degree three.  In particular, \emph{every} complete integral curve
$D\subset X_P$ projects to $\mathbb P^1$ with degree at most three.
Every degree-three curve other than $C$ has constant value $u=c\ne0$
satisfying
\begin{equation*}
 c=3B_P(c)^2,\qquad
 B_P(U)=\sum_{k\ge1}q_{3k+2}(-U)^k.
\end{equation*}
There are only finitely many such nonzero values $c$.
Properness is established independently in
\Cref{thm:p-projective-contraction}.
<!-- end proposition-13 -->
<!-- proof-30: body_md -->
On the $b$-chart write $w=w_2$ and
$u=-w^3-bQ(w)+b^2w_1$.  The inverse gluing gives
\[
 v_2=b^{-1}w,\qquad
 v_1=b^3w_1-3b^{-1}w^2-bw^3-b^2Q(w).
\]
Thus the first two terms of \eqref{eq:p-global-boundary-function}
expand as
\[
 a^2u-\frac13v_1v_2
 =w_1-b^{-1}Q(w)+\frac13w^4
   -\frac13b^2w_1w+\frac13bQ(w)w.
\]
For each $d\ge3$ the displayed definitions give
$T_d=b^{-1}w^d+O(b^0)$, where $O(b^0)$ is a polynomial in
$b,w_1,w$.  Hence the sum cancels the only negative power of $b$
and $F_P$ is regular on both charts.  Expanding $u^k$ one order
further shows uniformly in the three residue classes of $d$ that
\[
 T_d|_{b=0}\ \text{after removing }b^{-1}w^d
 =\left\lfloor\frac d3\right\rfloor w^{d-3}Q(w).
\]
This proves the formula for $\Theta_P$.  On $B$ the change of
coordinates $(w,w_1)\mapsto(w,F_P)$ is triangular.  Its map to
$(u,F_P)$ is then $(w,F_P)\mapsto(-w^3,F_P)$, a finite free
extension with basis $1,w,w^2$.
Now let $D\subset X_P$ be a complete integral curve.  Projection
to $\mathbb P^1$ is finite of degree $d>0$; since $D$ is integral,
the finite module $\pi_*\mathcal O_D$ is locally free of rank $d$.
Thus $D\cap B$ is a zero-dimensional scheme of length $d$.
Both $u$ and $F_P$ are constant on $D$, say $c$ and $f$.
The closed subscheme $D\cap B$ is contained in
$B\cap\{u=c,F_P=f\}$, whose coordinate ring is
$\mathbb C[w]/(w^3+c)$ and has length three.  Hence $d\le3$.
On the opposite affine plane $A=\{a=0\}\subset U_a$, put
$v=v_2$.  The definitions above give
\[
 u|_A=3v^2,\qquad
 F_P|_A=v\sum_{k\ge1}q_{3k+1}(-u)^k
           -\frac{v_1}{3}\bigl(v+B_P(u)\bigr).
\]
If $c\ne0$ and $c\ne3B_P(c)^2$, neither of the two roots of
$3v^2=c$ equals $-B_P(c)$.  Thus fixing $u=c,F_P=f$ determines
$v_1$ uniquely at each root; the scheme-theoretic fibre on $A$
has length two.  Since $D\cap A$ has length $d$ and is a closed
subscheme of that fibre, $d\le2$.  The case $c=0$ contains only
$C$ by \Cref{prop:p-zero-fibre-curves}.  Finally $B_P(0)=0$, so
$3B_P(U)^2-U$ is a nonzero polynomial (its linear term is $-U$),
with only finitely many nonzero roots.
<!-- end proof-30 -->
<!-- theorem-8: body_md -->
\label{thm:p-projective-contraction}
For every nonzero $P\in y^4\mathbb C[y]$, the threefold $X_P$ of
\eqref{eq:p-curve-glue} has a projective birational morphism
\[
 \rho_P:X_P\longrightarrow
 Y_P=\operatorname{Spec}H^0(X_P,\mathcal O_{X_P}).
\]
The target is a normal affine threefold, and the fibre over
$o=\rho_P(C)$ has support exactly $C$.  Near $o$ this is a small
crepant contraction onto a Gorenstein terminal threefold, and is
an isomorphism away from $C$.  Furthermore, $S_P$ is finitely generated and
$(S_P)_+^N\subseteq(s_0,s_1)S_P$ for some $N$.
<!-- end theorem-8 -->
<!-- proof-31: body_md -->
Write $Q(w)=P'(w)=\sum_{d\ge3}q_dw^d$ and retain the global
$u,F_P,T_d$ of \Cref{prop:p-global-boundary-coordinate}.  Define
\[
 A(U)=\sum_{k\ge1}q_{3k}(-U)^k,\quad
 B(U)=\sum_{k\ge1}q_{3k+2}(-U)^k,\quad
 D(U)=\sum_{k\ge1}q_{3k+1}(-U)^k,
\]
\[
 H(w,U)=A(U)+wD(U)+w^2B(U),\qquad
 K(w,U)=\frac{Q(w)-H(w,U)}{w^3+U}\in\mathbb C[w,U].
\]
The last inclusion follows by polynomial division.  On $U_a$ put
\begin{equation}\label{eq:p-third-global-function}
 \mathcal G_P=v_1^2+27av_2^3+9a^2v_1v_2
             +9\sum_{d\ge3}q_dT_{d+1}.
\end{equation}
After substitution on $U_b$, the first three terms have only
one negative Laurent coefficient, $-9b^{-1}wQ(w)$: their
$b^{-4}$ and $b^{-2}$ terms cancel.  Each $T_{d+1}$ has
negative term $b^{-1}w^{d+1}$ and no other negative term.
Thus $\mathcal G_P$ is global and
$\mathcal G_P|_{\{a=v_2=0\}}=v_1^2$.

Put $v=v_2$ on $U_a$.  Direct substitution gives
\begin{equation}\label{eq:p-f-a-monic}
 F_P=a^2u+aA(u)+vD(u)-\frac{v_1}{3}(v+B(u)).
\end{equation}
Using $av_1=u-3v^2$ and multiplying by $a$ yields
the following monic equation for $v$:
\begin{equation}\label{eq:p-v-monic}
 v^3+B(u)v^2-\frac{u}{3}v-\frac{uB(u)}3
 +a\bigl(a^2u+aA(u)+vD(u)-F_P\bigr)=0.
\end{equation}
Every $T_{d+1}$ is at most linear in $v_1$ over
$\mathbb C[a,u,v]$.  Equation \eqref{eq:p-third-global-function}
is therefore a monic quadratic for $v_1$ over
$\mathbb C[a,u,F_P,\mathcal G_P,v]$.  Consequently
$\mathbb C[a,v,v_1]$ is finite over
$\mathbb C[a,u,F_P,\mathcal G_P]$.

On $U_b$ let $w=w_2$, $z=w_1$.  The identity
$v_1=bu-3b^{-1}w^2$ gives
\[
 F_P=b^{-2}(u+w^3)-\frac{uw}{3}
            +b^{-1}H(w,u)-\frac{buB(u)}3.
\]
Clearing denominators gives a monic cubic for $w$:
\begin{equation}\label{eq:p-w-monic}
 w^3+bw^2B(u)+bwD(u)+bA(u)+u
       -\frac{b^2uw}{3}-\frac{b^3uB(u)}3-b^2F_P=0.
\end{equation}
For $R=F_P+uw/3+buB(u)/3$ we have
$u+w^3+bH=b^2R$.  Combining
$u+w^3+bQ=b^2z$ with $Q=H+(w^3+u)K$ gives the
polynomial formula
\begin{equation}\label{eq:p-z-polynomial}
 z=(1+bK(w,u))R-K(w,u)H(w,u).
\end{equation}
Thus $\mathbb C[b,w,z]$ is finite over
$\mathbb C[b,u,F_P]$, and in particular over
$\mathbb C[b,u,F_P,\mathcal G_P]$.  Finiteness on the two
standard base charts proves that
\[
 (\pi,u,F_P,\mathcal G_P):
 X_P\longrightarrow\mathbb P^1\times\mathbb A^3
\]
is finite.  Its composition $h=(u,F_P,\mathcal G_P)$
with the projective projection is projective.  At
$(a,v,v_1)=(0,0,t)$, $t\ne0$, the Jacobian of $h$ has
determinant $-2t^3/3$; hence $h$ is dominant and
generically finite.

Set $R_P=H^0(X_P,\mathcal O_{X_P})$.  Proper pushforward
makes $R_P$ finite over $\mathbb C[u,F_P,\mathcal G_P]$.
On the generic point of $\mathbb A^3$, the fibre is a
finite integral scheme, so localization of $R_P$ there
has fraction field $\mathbb C(X_P)$.  Moreover
$R_P=B_a\cap B_b$ is normal.  Stein factorization now
gives the stated projective birational $\rho_P$ and a
finite $Y_P\to\mathbb A^3$.

The common zero set of $u,F_P,\mathcal G_P$ is $C$.
On $a\ne0$, $u=0$ implies $v_1=-3v^2/a$ and
\eqref{eq:p-f-a-monic} gives $F_P=v^3/a$.
On $a=0$, $u=0$ implies $v=0$ and then
$\mathcal G_P=v_1^2$.  On $b=0$, $u=-w^3$
and $F_P=z+\Theta_P(w)$.  These observations prove the
assertion, including at both ends of $C$.
Surjectivity of the Stein morphism shows that there is
only one point of $Y_P$ over the origin of $\mathbb A^3$,
and its fibre under $\rho_P$ is supported on $C$.

By \Cref{cor:p-isolate-all-curves}, after restricting to
a principal neighbourhood of $o$, every complete curve
in $X_P$ is $C$.  Thus every other fibre of the projective
birational map is zero-dimensional; it is finite and hence
an isomorphism there by normality of $Y_P$.  The exceptional
locus is $C$, so the map is small.  The transition Jacobian
of \eqref{eq:p-curve-glue} is a nonzero constant, making
$K_{X_P}$ trivial.  The small map transfers this rational
volume form to a Cartier canonical divisor on $Y_P$ and
$K_{X_P}=\rho_P^*K_{Y_P}$.  Every exceptional divisorial
valuation over the smooth $X_P$ has positive discrepancy,
so $Y_P$ is terminal; terminal singularities are
Cohen--Macaulay, and the Cartier canonical divisor makes
it Gorenstein.

{
For clarity, the neighbourhood and discrepancy assertions can be
checked without assuming properness of an arbitrary curve
neighbourhood.  Let $K_P$ be the polynomial of
\Cref{cor:p-isolate-all-curves} and put $h=K_P(u)\in R_P$.
Since $h(o)=K_P(0)\ne0$, restriction of the projective Stein map
to $Y_P[h^{-1}]$ retains $C$.  Every positive-dimensional fibre
contains a complete integral curve, while
$X_P[h^{-1}]$ has no such curve besides $C$.
Thus the map is quasi-finite over $Y_P[h^{-1}]\setminus\{o\}$;
projective plus quasi-finite is finite, and a finite birational
map to this normal open is an isomorphism.  In particular no
exceptional divisor occurs near $o$.

The Jacobian of the coordinate change
$(a,v_2,v_1)\mapsto(b,w_2,w_1)$ equals $-1$, so the nowhere-zero
three-form on $X_P$ descends over the isomorphism locus.
The complement of that locus in $Y_P[h^{-1}]$ has codimension three.
Normality extends the descended form as a generator of the
reflexive canonical sheaf; hence $K_{Y_P}$ is Cartier and
$K_{X_P}=\rho_P^*K_{Y_P}$.  If a divisorial valuation has centre
in the exceptional point on $Y_P$, its centre on the smooth
$X_P$ is not a divisor, because $\rho_P$ is small.  Its discrepancy
is therefore the strictly positive discrepancy over a smooth
threefold.  This establishes terminality at $o$ and, since
terminal singularities are rational, the Cohen--Macaulay property
needed for the Gorenstein assertion.  The argument also makes clear
why the other complete curves on the full $X_P$ do not interfere
with the local contraction.
}

Finally $X_P\to\mathbb P^1\times Y_P$ is finite.
Hence $L=\pi^*\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^1}(1)$ is
relatively ample, $S_P$ is finitely generated over $R_P$,
and $X_P\simeq\operatorname{Proj}S_P$.
The two opens $D_+(s_0),D_+(s_1)$ cover this Proj,
so $(S_P)_+\subseteq\sqrt{(s_0,s_1)}$ and finite
generation supplies the exponent $N$.
<!-- end proof-31 -->
<!-- proposition-14: body_md -->
\label{prop:p-zero-divisorial}
For $P=0$, the three global functions
$u,F_0,\mathcal G_0$ still give a projective affinization
$X_0\to\operatorname{Spec}H^0(X_0,\mathcal O_{X_0})$.
It is divisorial in every neighbourhood of $C$: a divisor
containing $C$ is swept out by complete integral double
sections.  Thus the nonzero-parameter hypothesis in the
smallness assertion of \cref{thm:p-projective-contraction}
is necessary.
<!-- end proposition-14 -->
<!-- proof-32: body_md -->
The monic equations \eqref{eq:p-v-monic} and
\eqref{eq:p-w-monic}, the polynomial expression
\eqref{eq:p-z-polynomial}, and the Jacobian calculation in
the proof of \cref{thm:p-projective-contraction} remain valid
when all $q_d$ vanish.  They prove projectivity and the
birational Stein factorization for $P=0$.

For each $k\in\mathbb C^\times$ set $c=-k^3$.  On the
$a$-chart define
\[
 v_2^2+ka v_2+k^2a^2+\frac{k^3}{3}=0,\qquad
 v_1=3kv_2+3k^2a.
\]
On the $b$-chart the same curve is defined by
\[
 w_2^2+kw_2+k^2+\frac{k^3}{3}b^2=0,\qquad
 w_1=-\frac{k^3}{3}(w_2-k).
\]
The two descriptions agree on the overlap: the first
quadratic gives $u=c$, and on the second chart
$w_2^3+c=(w_2-k)(w_2^2+kw_2+k^2)$ gives
$b^2w_1=w_2^3+c$.  Both quadratics are monic, so these
curves are finite flat of degree two over $\mathbb P^1$.
Their discriminant is not a square over $\mathbb C(a)$
for $k\ne0$, hence they are integral.  At $k=0$ the same
equations have underlying support $C$.

Let $E$ be the closure of their union in $X_0$.
The parameter $k$ varies in one dimension and the values
$u|_{D_k}=-k^3$ vary, so $E$ has dimension two and
contains $C$.  Every regular function on $X_0$ is constant
on each complete $D_k$.  Thus the affinization maps $E$
to a curve, contracting a divisor through $C$.
<!-- end proof-32 -->
<!-- corollary-6: body_md -->
\label{cor:p-formal-flop-realization}
For every $p(y)\in y^4\mathbb C[[y]]$ of finite order,
there is a smooth threefold flop with contraction algebra $A_p$.
In particular $A_p$ is symmetric and four-periodic as a
bimodule. The uniqueness and GV statements will then follow
from \Cref{thm:full-p,thm:gv-all-n}.
<!-- end corollary-6 -->
<!-- proof-33: body_md -->
Choose a sufficiently long polynomial truncation $P$.
By the finite-truncation assertion of \Cref{lem:poly-realization},
$A_P\simeq A_p$; by
\Cref{prop:p-geometric-neighbourhood} and \Cref{thm:p-projective-contraction},
$A_P$ is the contraction algebra of a smooth local flop.
Symmetry and bimodule four-periodicity are the standard
properties of this contraction algebra \cite{JKM}. No exact length
formula, centre formula, or uniqueness assertion is used to construct the flop.
<!-- end proof-33 -->
<!-- corollary-7: body_md -->
\label{cor:p-isolate-all-curves}
For each nonzero polynomial $P\in y^4\mathbb C[y]$, there is an explicit
polynomial $K_P(U)$ with $K_P(0)\ne0$ such that
$\{K_P(u)\ne0\}\subset X_P$ contains $C$ and no other complete
integral curve.  One can take the product of $H_P(U)$ in
\Cref{prop:p-all-double-sections} with
\[
 \prod_{\substack{c\ne0\\ c=3B_P(c)^2}}(U-c),
\]
listing each distinct factor once.  The independent finite-map
argument of \Cref{thm:p-projective-contraction} proves properness.
<!-- end corollary-7 -->
<!-- proof-34: body_md -->
Every complete integral curve has degree at most three by
\Cref{prop:p-global-boundary-coordinate}.  Degrees one and two
are removed by $H_P$, while the displayed finite product removes
every possible degree-three value of $u$.  All excluded values
are nonzero, so the open set retains $C$.
<!-- end proof-34 -->
<!-- lemma-8: body_md -->
\label{lem:jac-dt-conservation}
Suppose the polynomial Jacobi algebra of a one-parameter polynomial
potential has a finite locally free direct factor over a henselian
neighborhood of $t=0$.  Write $\mathcal D$ for its completion and
$D_0$ for its special fibre.  Then, after
extension of the fraction field to an algebraic closure, for every
$j\ge1$ one has
\[
  \operatorname{DT}_j(D_0)
  =\operatorname{DT}_j(\mathcal D_{\overline{\Bbbk((t))}}).
\]
The assertion concerns the isolated factor followed in the deformation;
other critical points of the polynomial potential play no role.
<!-- end lemma-8 -->
<!-- proof-35: body_md -->
Let $U_j$ be the smooth relative scheme of triples $(X,Y,v)$ with
$v$ cyclic for $X,Y$, modulo the free $\mathrm{GL}_j$ action.  The
trace of the polynomial potential is a function $F$ on $U_j$.  The
cyclic derivatives and nondegeneracy of the trace pairing give a
scheme-theoretic identity
\[
  \operatorname{Hilb}_j(\operatorname{Jac}(W_t))
      =\operatorname{Crit}_{U_j}(F_t).
\]
The part corresponding to $\mathcal D$ is an open-and-closed part of
this critical locus.  It is projective over the base: it is the
closed scheme of rank-$j$ quotient modules of the finite free algebra
$\mathcal D$, inside its relative Grassmannian.

Restrict the relative critical-locus obstruction theory
\( [T_{U_j/S}|_H\xrightarrow{\mathrm{Hess}(F)}
                      \Omega_{U_j/S}|_H] \)
to this proper part $H$.  The localized top Chern class of the
relative one-form $d_{U_j/S}F$ specializes to the corresponding class
on either fibre \cite{BF1997}.  On each fibre its degree is the
intrinsic Behrend-weighted Euler characteristic of the critical locus
\cite{Behrend2009}.  Proper pushforward therefore makes these degrees
equal.  Flatness of the Hilbert scheme itself is not required.

{
Here is the precise specialization behind the preceding sentence.
Work over a smooth henselian trait $S$ on which the polynomial
Jacobi algebra has the stated finite direct factor $\mathcal D$.
The idempotent projecting to $\mathcal D$ acts on a flat rank-$j$
cyclic quotient as an idempotent matrix; the condition that its rank
is $j$ is open and closed.  Hence the pure-$\mathcal D$ locus $H$
is an open-and-closed component of the relative critical scheme.
It is proper over $S$: a cyclic quotient of $\mathcal D$ is a
left-ideal quotient, and the left-ideal condition cuts out a
closed subscheme of the relative Grassmannian of the finite locally
free module $\mathcal D$.

Let $r=\dim(U_j/S)=j^2+j$ and $E=\Omega_{U_j/S}$.
The zero scheme of $s=d_{U_j/S}F\in\Gamma(U_j,E)$ is the relative
critical scheme.  The localized top Chern class of $(E,s)$,
restricted to its open-and-closed component $H$, defines
$\alpha\in A_1(H)$.  Write $j^*\alpha$ for restriction to the
generic fibre and $i_0^!\alpha$ for the refined pullback to the
closed fibre.  Compatibility of the zero-section Gysin map with
both operations gives, for $\xi=\eta,0$ respectively,
\[
 \alpha_\xi
 =c_r(E_\xi,s_\xi)\cap[U_{j,\xi}]\big|_{H_\xi}
 \in A_0(H_\xi).
\]
This is the fibrewise critical-locus virtual class
\cite[\S14.1]{Fulton1998}\cite{BF1997}.  Since $H\to S$ is proper,
its pushforward is $m[S]\in A_1(S)$ for one integer $m$.
Generic restriction and refined special pullback commute with
proper pushforward, so the degrees of both displayed zero-cycles
equal $m$.  Finally the
critical obstruction theory
$[T_{U_{j,\xi}}|_{H_\xi}\to\Omega_{U_{j,\xi}}|_{H_\xi}]$
is symmetric; Behrend's degree theorem identifies its virtual
degree with $\chi(H_\xi,\nu_{H_\xi})$ \cite{Behrend2009}.
This also explains why neither flatness of $H/S$ nor constancy of
its ordinary Euler characteristic is being assumed.
}
<!-- end proof-35 -->
<!-- lemma-9: body_md -->
\label{lem:poly-realization}
Let $p\in\Bbbk[[y]]$ have initial order $n\ge4$, and let $d=\dim A_p<\infty$.  If $P$ is a polynomial truncation
of $p$ through degree $N>d+2$, then $A_P\cong A_p$.  Moreover the
finite free smoothing of $A_P$ in \eqref{ap:eq:deformation} is the
completion of an isolated factor of a polynomial Jacobi family.
<!-- end lemma-9 -->
<!-- proof-36: body_md -->
The radical of the local algebra $A_p$ satisfies $J^d=0$.
The derivatives of $p$ and $P$ differ by an element of
$(x,y)^{d+1}$. Applying \Cref{ap:lem:jets} proves equality
of the two closed Jacobi ideals. This argument uses only finite
dimensionality, independently of the centre computation.

For completeness, the polynomial perturbation really has a finite
algebraic factor.  Put $z=y^3=-3x^2$ and write the polynomial
$y$-derivative, including its $t$ terms, as
$q_t(y)=a_t(z)+yb_t(z)+y^2c_t(z)$.  The four rewriting rules preceding
\Cref{ap:prop:overlap} span its polynomial Jacobi algebra over
$\Bbbk[t,z]$ by the same twelve words.  On a geometric fibre with
$z\ne0$, a simple module has dimension at most three.  Its possible
$z$-values are roots of monic polynomials over $\Bbbk[t]$: in dimension
one use the resultant of $y^3-z$ and $q_t(y)^2+3y^7$; in dimension
two use the resultant of $y^3-z$ and
\[
 q_t(y)+\omega q_t(\omega y),\qquad \omega^3=1\ne\omega;
\]
and in dimension three use $z+3c_t(z)^2$. Indeed $X^2=-z/3$
has two distinct eigenvalues when $z\ne0$; $X$ cannot be scalar
in a three-dimensional simple module. Their multiplicities are
therefore two and one, and $\operatorname{tr}X=-c_t(z)$ is
one of $\pm\sqrt{-z/3}$, giving the stated polynomial.  The leading coefficients
of the first two resultants are nonzero constants: the polynomial
$q_t$ has leading $y$-coefficient independent of $t$, and
$1+\omega^m\ne0$ for every integer $m$.  The third polynomial also
has a nonzero constant leading coefficient.  The value $z=0$ is
accounted for by multiplying these polynomials by $z$.  Hence the
support of the twelve-generated $\Bbbk[t,z]$-module lies over the zero
locus of a polynomial monic in $z$; a power of that polynomial
annihilates the module.  The polynomial Jacobi algebra is therefore
finite over $\Bbbk[t]$ near $t=0$.  Its special-fibre factor supported
at $(x,y)=(0,0)$ splits off after henselization and completes to the
family in \eqref{ap:eq:deformation}.  Its freeness is exactly
\Cref{ap:thm:all-parameters}.
{
Here is the factor and completion argument explicitly.  Put
$R=\Bbbk[t]_{(t)}^{\mathrm h}$ and let $B$ be the polynomial
Jacobi algebra over $R$.  The preceding monic annihilator makes
$B$ a finite $R$-module.  In $B/tB$, the central character $z=0$
has only the simple module $x=y=0$.  Indeed, setting $z=0$ gives
$x^2=y^3=0$ and $xy^2+yxy+y^2x=0$.  The twelve-word spanning
bound makes a simple module at most three-dimensional.  If
$Y^2=0$, then $YXY=0$ and the ideal generated by $X,Y$ is
nilpotent.  In the remaining three-dimensional case put
$Y=E_{12}+E_{23}$.  The displayed relation forces
$X_{31}=0$ and $X_{32}=-X_{21}$; the $(3,1)$ entry of
$X^2=0$ then gives $X_{21}=X_{32}=0$.  Hence $X$ and $Y$
are simultaneously upper triangular, which precludes a
nontrivial simple module.

Choose a monic polynomial $f(Z)\in R[Z]$ annihilating the action
of $z$ on $B$, and write its special fibre as
$f_0(Z)=Z^e g(Z)$ with $g(0)\ne0$.  Hensel factorization of
these coprime factors and the Chinese remainder theorem give
a central idempotent in $R[z]/(f)$ and therefore a direct factor
$D\subset B$ whose special fibre is precisely the block at
$x=y=0$.  This fibre is $A_P$: its augmentation-adic
completion changes nothing because the finite block has
nilpotent radical.  Completing $D$ in $t$ is the same as
completing the polynomial Jacobi presentation in $(t,x,y)$,
since $x,y$ are radical modulo $t$; thus
$\widehat D\cong\mathcal A_P$.  By
\Cref{ap:thm:all-parameters}, $\widehat D$ is free of rank $d$
over $\Bbbk[[t]]$.  Faithful flatness of
$R\longrightarrow\Bbbk[[t]]$ and finiteness of $D$ imply that
$D$ is finite free of rank $d$ over the local ring $R$.
}
<!-- end proof-36 -->
<!-- theorem-9: body_md -->
\label{thm:gv-all-n}
Let $\Bbbk=\mathbb C$.  Suppose $A_p$ in Theorem \ref{thm:full-p} is the contraction algebra of a
smooth threefold flop with a single smooth exceptional curve.  Its
geometric genus-zero GV invariants are
\[
 (n_1,n_2,n_3)=
 \begin{cases}(6,3,1),&n=4,\\(7,n-1,1),&n\ge5.\end{cases}
\]
All invariants $n_j$ with $j>3$ vanish.
<!-- end theorem-9 -->
<!-- proof-37: body_md -->
By Lemmas \ref{lem:poly-realization} and \ref{lem:jac-dt-conservation} and Theorem 
\ref{thm:full-p}, the DT series of $A_p$ equals that of its displayed
split semisimple smoothing $S$.  For one factor $\operatorname{M}_m(\Bbbk)$,
the cyclic modules of dimension $mr$ form $\operatorname{Gr}(r,m)$.
Its Behrend-weighted Euler characteristic is
$(-1)^{r(m-r)}\binom mr$.  Multiplication over the factors gives
\[
 1+\sum_{j\ge1}\operatorname{DT}_j(A_p)u^j
 =\prod_{m=1}^{3}\bigl(1-(-1)^m u^m\bigr)^{m b_m},
 \qquad
 (b_1,b_2,b_3)=
 \begin{cases}(6,3,1),&n=4,\\(7,n-1,1),&n\ge5.\end{cases}
\]
Hua--Toda's theorem identifies the same series for a smooth flop
with $\prod_{m\ge1}(1-(-1)^mu^m)^{mn_m}$
\cite[Theorem~4.4]{HT2018}.  Comparison of coefficients, or unique
factorization of this formal Euler product, yields $n_m=b_m$ for
all $m$.  More explicitly, when $n\ge5$ the first coefficients are
\[
 \operatorname{DT}_1(A_p)=7,
 \qquad \operatorname{DT}_2(A_p)=\binom72-2(n-1)=23-2n,
 \qquad \operatorname{DT}_3(A_p)=52-14n.
\]
Thus $n_1=7$ and
$23-2n=\binom{n_1}{2}-2n_2$, whence $n_2=n-1$.
Finally $\dim A_p=\sum_m m^2n_m=4n+12$
\cite[Theorem~4.1]{HT2018}; since comparison of the full Euler products has already excluded
blocks of size greater than three,
$n_3=1$.  The $n=4$ computation similarly gives $(6,3,1)$.
<!-- end proof-37 -->
<!-- proposition-15: body_md -->
\label{prop:intrinsic-gate}
For any $p$ in \cref{thm:full-p}, the equality
